strengths: The paper addresses an important efficiency bottleneck in multimodal models: the large visual prefix processed by the language model. Combining attention-based selection, token merging, and spatial coverage provides a simple, practically relevant approach without adding a learned compression network.

PruMerge+ demonstrates a useful accuracy–compression tradeoff. At 25% of visual tokens, the 7B model achieves 76.8 versus 78.5 on VQAv2 and 64.9 versus 64.3 on MMBench (Table 1). Such savings can be valuable despite modest accuracy losses.

Evaluation covers six image benchmarks, two language-model sizes, and three video benchmarks. The Video-LLaVA experiments are particularly encouraging because compression preserves comparable performance without additional training (Table 3).

The ablations provide evidence for informed selection and token supplementation: PruMerge outperforms uniform sampling in Table 4, while adding token supplementation improves MME from 1221.6 to 1350.3 in Table 5. The pipeline figures help explain the approach, and the principal underlying models, training data, and related token-reduction methods are cited.
weaknesses: Practical acceleration remains insufficiently established for an efficiency-centered contribution. Table 2 reports roofline estimates rather than measured latency, and does not establish end-to-end savings including the visual encoder, compression overhead, and decoding. It also does not evaluate the PruMerge+ setting with the strongest accuracy retention. Moreover, the claimed O(n) clustering complexity conflicts with the all-pairs key similarities in Eq. 4; restricting comparisons to m anchors still requires O(mn), which is quadratic at a fixed retained fraction.

The algorithm specification contains consequential reproducibility ambiguities. Algorithm 1 adds m spatial tokens to m selected tokens, which does not explain the reported increase from 5.5% retention for PruMerge to 25% for PruMerge+. Its subsequent loop and output still reference only m tokens. The neighborhood size k is not supplied, and the unnormalized sum in line 10 is not reconciled with the description of weighted averaging. These details affect both representations and the reported computational budgets.

The experiments do not isolate the central benefit of adaptive IQR selection. A fixed top-k attention baseline with identical merging and a matched average token budget is missing. Table 7 also does not clearly establish whether ToMe, ATS, and EViT receive the same LoRA adaptation as PruMerge+, while CrossGet results are imported from another paper. Consequently, the comparisons leave uncertainty about how much improvement comes from the proposed selection rule versus adaptation and implementation choices.

The performance-preservation claims exceed the evidence for aggressive compression. In Table 1, 7B PruMerge reduces VQAv2 from 78.5 to 72.0, POPE from 85.9 to 76.3, and MME from 1510.7 to 1350.3. Section 4.1 also claims improved POPE performance although all proposed image-model variants score below their baselines. These losses can still constitute a useful compression tradeoff, but should be distinguished from the substantially better retention achieved by PruMerge+.
